# Assessment of owl limpet (*Lottia gigantea*) populations at sites within Crystal Cove State Marine Conservation Area

```{r load packages, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
```

## Project Summary: 

*Once you have completed this entire assignment, come back and write a project summary here that covers the aims, research questions, and basic methods of this study.*

This study analyzes the territory dynamics and size distributions of owl limpets across rocky inter tidal sites along the Crystal Cove State Conservation Area. Owl limpets play a keystone role in the structure of inter tidal communities through their establishment and defending of algae communities from predators. Field data was collected across the span of 3 years from populations across Corona del Mar, Treasure Cove, Shaws Cove, and Heisler Park, all of whom experienced varying levels of human disturbance. This study looks at how human impact changes limpet demography and whether individual body size and territory size scale together.

Research Questions:

1.  Do owl limpet shell sizes differ significantly between high human impact sites and low human impact sites? How do sizes vary across years.
2.  Does owl limpet density differ significantly between high human impact sites and low human impact sites?
3.  What is the relationship between limpet body mass and defended territory area?

Basic Methods:

Surveys of owl limpets were taken in 4 different sites with varying human impact at the mid to upper rocky intertidal zone. Transects were used to record limpet size and density, and all owl limpets measuring \>15 mm were measured along their longest axis. As transect lengths were 2 meters, density was calculated with the formula count/(transect length \* 2). Defended territory area was measured using a mesh quadrat of 19 x 19 mm cells laid directly over the territory to count the squares. Individual body mass was calculated using shell length based on the equation mass_g = 0.00009\*length \^ 3.0471. Log transformations were used to make the data linear and stabilize variance. Best fit linear regressions of both the class data and Fenberg data sets were extracted for comparison.

You have been given data from several locations and survey years:

- 2022: Corona del Mar (CDM) - size data only, taken haphazardly

- 2023: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

- 2024: Heisler Park and Shaws Cove - size data in variable length transects, territories

- 2025: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

```{r}
SizeData_2022_2025
```

#### 2.2 What was the limpet density (i.e., limpets per square meter) for each transect?

Make a new dataframe out of the `No_CDM_Sizes` that has a column called *density,* that calculates the limpets per square meter for each transect. Remember that the transect included 1 meter on either side of the tape (total of 2 meters wide). Make sure to maintain the separation in year for the two Treasure Cove surveys using the `group_by()` function.

```{r}
Limpet_Density <- No_CDM_Sizes |> 
  group_by(site, year, transect_num, transect_length_m) |> 
  summarize(count = n()) |> #Aggregates data by counting up # rows for each unique transect
  mutate(density = count / (transect_length_m * 2)) #Calculates limpet density/square meter fior each transect
  
  

Limpet_Density
```

Do you see any patterns just from examining this table of values?

Limpet density seems much lower on average in Treasure Cove compared to Heisler Park and Shaws Cove. Shaws Cove also seems to have an even higher average density than Heisler Park.

#### 2.2. Calculating mean and standard error of population density

What was the mean limpets per square meter across all sites? And the standard deviation? And standard error?

```{r}

mean_density = mean(Limpet_Density$density, na.rm = TRUE) #Takes the mean of the density column in the Limpet Density df

standard_dev_density = sd(Limpet_Density$density, na.rm = TRUE) #Takes the standard deviation of the density column

standard_error_density = standard_dev_density / sqrt(length(Limpet_Density$density)) #Calculates standard error from mean and standard deviation


mean_density

standard_dev_density

standard_error_density

```

Now create a summary table in which you calculate separate mean and standard deviation for each site and year (Shaws vs. Heisler vs. Treasure Cove)? What was the standard error? Round the mean and standard error to one decimal place. (look up the `round()` function!)

```{r}
# use summarize() to calculate the mean and standard error (sd/sqrt(n)) for the two locations
LimpetPopSummary <- Limpet_Density |> #Summarize takes above methodology and applies it to all sites
  group_by(site, year) |> 
  summarize(
    mean_density = round(mean(density, na.rm = TRUE), 1), 
    standard_dev_density = sd(density, na.rm = TRUE),
    total = n(),
    standard_error_density = round(standard_dev_density / sqrt(total), 1)
  ) 
  
  
  
  
 
# Display your summary nicely using kable(). 
knitr::kable(LimpetPopSummary)
```

Based on these plots, does your data meet assumptions for a t-test?

No, the variability in the data from each group differs significantly. Looking at the boxplot, the median lines and whiskers also indicate the distribution is not normal as well. Thus our data does not meet the assumptions for a t-test.

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)?

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population?

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)?

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

#### 2.6. Does average number of owl limpets per square meter differ significantly between Heisler Park and Shaws Cove?

Filter the data to only include those sites before putting it into the `t.test()` function. These are a good comparison because they were measured in the same year with the same survey methods.

```{r t-test}
# run a t-test on your count data from each site (Limpet_Density)
ShawsHeislerDensity <- Limpet_Density |> 
  filter(site != "Treasure Cove")


t.test(density ~ site, data = ShawsHeislerDensity) #Runs a t-test comparing site and density without considering Treasure Cove data)

```

Explain the results of this t-test. Are you surprised by this result, given the figure you made above? Why do you think the results are what they are?

The result of this t-test fails to reject the null hypothesis that the average number of owl limpets per square meter does not differ significantly between the two parks. The p value of .2629 tells us that there is a 26% chance the difference we observed between site densities(t = -1.1649) was obtained purely by chance through random sampling. This didn't surprise me, given that when I made the figures above the error bars of the two sites on my column plot actually overlapped. This was already a big hint that the difference in the sites' observed densities was not statistically significant.

#### 3.2. Is there a [statistically significant]{.underline} difference in [mean]{.underline} size between limpets measured at Treasure Cove (a relatively low-impact site) compared to CDM (a high impact site)?

We have a much larger sample size for shell lengths than we did for density, so we can apply our tests of assumptions more rigorously and demonstrate our various tests.

##### 3.2.1 [Determine whether a parametric or non-parametric test is appropriate.]{.underline}

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)? **YES**

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population? **(Yes)**

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)? **NO**

```{r}
## Test for Homogeneity of Variance with an F-Test

# create the appropriate filter to include only Treasure Cove and CDM data
CDM_TC_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |> 
  filter(site == "Corona del Mar" | site == "Treasure Cove")

  
# set the linear model for testing the assumptions
model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)

# Examine plot of Residuals vs. Fitted values
plot(model, which = 1)

# F-test for homogeneity of variance - if p-value < 0.05 then variances are different. 
var.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)

# NOTE: if your sample fails this test, have no fear! Welch's t-test (the default that R uses) is okay to use with unequal variances. 

```

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

```{r}
## Test for normality

# examine a QQ-plot
plot(model, which = 2)

# conduct a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals
shapiro.test(model$residuals)
```

Why will we not pay attention to this Shapiro-Wilk test result? Because the sample size is very large and Shapiro-Wilk is overly sensitive (gives false positives) at large sample sizes.

##### 3.2.2 [Conduct the test]{.underline}

```{r t-test or Wilcox}
# calculate the t-test results
t.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)
```

#### 4.1 Territory Data

Clean up and combine the 2023, 2024 and 2025 data for Territories:


#### 4.2 How many limpet territories did we measure?

```{r}
## How many territories were measured at each site in each year? 
All_Territories |> nrow()
```

#### 4.3 Calculate meaningful variables from our measured values

Create new columns for:

- territory area in square millimeters from the "`numbsquares`" column

- Limpet body mass from shell length (equation below is from Fenberg et al. 2013).

```{r}
All_Territories_area_mass <- All_Territories |> 
  mutate(
    territory_size_mm2 = numbsquares * (19 * 19),  # create new column for territory area in mm^2 using "numbsquares" column
    body_mass = .00009 * (size_mm ^ 3.0471)  # create a new column for limpet body mass, formula: mass_g = 0.00009*length ^ 3.0471
  )
```

Explore the relationship between mass_g, and area_mm2 using scatter plots.

```{r}
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "pink") + #Creates a regression line across scatter plot, hiding the SE zone
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Territory Size (mm^2)")
  
  
```

#### 4.6. What important assumptions of tests of linear regression do these scatter plots fail? How can you tell?

```{r}

# write a linear model for the relationship, then use the plot() function on the model object to show the residuals vs. fitted values and QQ plots to assess your regression. 

linear_model <- lm(body_mass ~ territory_size_mm2, data = All_Territories_area_mass)

plot(linear_model) # Generates plots to verify linear model, including a residuals vs fitted plot, a Q-Q plot, a scale location plot, and a residuals vs leverage plot
```

One way to transform data that has this shape is to apply a log-transformation. Logarithmic relationships are common in biology for mass, volume, or other spatial relationships.

#### 4.7. Plot the relationship between log-transformed mass and log-transformed area. Does this relationship meet assumptions?

```{r scatterplot with regression line}
# plot a scatterplot log area on y axis by log mass_g on x axis, best fit regression line but no SE interval

All_Territories_area_mass |> ggplot() + 
  aes(x = log(body_mass), y = log(territory_size_mm2)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "pink") + 
  labs(x = "Log-transformed mass", y = "Log-transformed area")

```

```{r}
# write the linear model object and examine the residual and QQ plots
log_model <- lm(log(territory_size_mm2) ~ log(body_mass), data = All_Territories_area_mass)
  
plot(log_model, which = 1) #Creates a residuals vs fitted values plot
plot(log_model, which = 2) # Creates a Q-Q residuals plot
```

#### 4.8. What is the formula for the best fit line for the relationship between territory size and body mass in owl limpets?

```{r linear regression test summary}

log_model

#log(body_mass) = 0.505 * log(territory_size_mm2) - 3.106

```

**The formula for the best fit line can be extracted from the model summary. The two values in the Estimate column are the coefficients - (Intercept) gives the y-intercept, and the variable gives the slope.**

**log(area) = 0.8903 \* log(mass) + 8.2116**

**or**

**Y = 0.8903 + 8.2116**

#### 4.9 Compare the relationship we found to the original study.

```{r}
FenbergTerr

# Plot the Fenberg data with the log transformations
FenbergTerr |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = log(mass_g), y = log(area_mm2)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "pink") + 
  labs(x = "Log-transformed mass", y = "Log-transformed area")
 

# Find the slope and intercept of the best fit line
Fenberg_model <- lm(log(area_mm2) ~ log(mass_g), data = FenbergTerr)

Fenberg_model


```

Explain your findings!

Both the class collected data on owl limpets and the Fenberg data set show strong positive correlation between limpet body mass and territory size(p \< .001). The slope of the best fit line(0.8903) produced by class data was also very close to that produced by the Fenberg data set. Both data sets demonstrate that owl limpet size plays a significant role in territory area variation, although the Fenberg et al. observed a tighter fit in their data(R\^2 = .76, p \< .001), meaning over 3/4 of variation in territory size was occuring due to body mass. In compatison our class data is more widely scattered, even if it is still statisitically significant. This can be explained by the fact that the class data was sampled across multiple sites that were differing in multiple environmental variables. Because the data was transformed with a log transformation, the relationship between limpet size and territory size is not linear. Rather, as limpet size increases territory size increases at a decreasing rate.

Overall our findings in the class data validate Fenberg et al.'s own findings, that owl limpet territory size is strongly controlled by size/body mass.
